title: Reliance and Rolls-Royce Partner to Build Engine for India's Fifth-Generation Fighter Jet
excerpt: The collaboration will co-develop a 120 kN-class engine for India's AMCA stealth fighter, with full technology transfer and Indian ownership of all intellectual property.
body:
• Reliance Industries and Rolls-Royce are partnering to co-develop a 120 kN-class engine for India's AMCA fifth-generation stealth fighter
  • The deal includes 100% technology transfer with all intellectual property remaining with India
  • If a contract is signed by end of 2026, engine core testing could begin by 2030, with serial production targeted for 2036
  • The estimated investment is $4.5 to $5 billion, placing India in an elite group of nations capable of building advanced jet engines

Reliance Industries and British aerospace giant Rolls-Royce have agreed to partner on developing a next-generation fighter jet engine for India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) — the country's flagship fifth-generation stealth fighter program. The collaboration marks a milestone in India's decades-long quest to build indigenous military aviation capabilities.

The Engine Challenge

The AMCA, being developed by India's Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and its Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA), is designed to feature advanced stealth technology, supercruise capability, and cutting-edge avionics. While the initial AMCA Mk1 prototypes will fly using American GE F414 engines producing about 98 kN of thrust, the more advanced Mk2 variant requires a significantly more powerful engine in the 110-130 kN thrust class.

This is where Rolls-Royce comes in. The company, which builds engines for the Eurofighter Typhoon and is a key partner in the UK's sixth-generation Tempest fighter program, has submitted a final proposal to jointly design, develop, and manufacture a new 120 kN-plus thrust engine with India.

Full Technology Transfer

The deal's most significant feature is its intellectual property structure. Rolls-Royce has committed to 100% transfer of technology, with all IP generated during the program remaining with India. This goes beyond traditional licensed manufacturing and represents a genuine co-development partnership.

"We will fully transfer technology, we will develop IP in India, and regarding the transfer of know-how for background knowledge, we will work in a way in which the Indian government, the UK government and Rolls-Royce are satisfied."

— Sashi Mukundan, Executive Vice President, Rolls-Royce India

Reliance's role as the Indian private-sector partner adds industrial heft to the project. Rolls-Royce has been in talks with multiple Indian companies and has proposed establishing a dedicated aero-engine design center within India to support the co-development effort. The partnership aligns with Reliance's growing defense portfolio and India's Aatmanirbhar Bharat (self-reliant India) initiative.

Development Timeline

Under the proposed schedule, contingent on a contract being finalized by end of 2026, the program would follow this roadmap:

Engine core testing, including the hot section, would begin by 2030. The first flight test of the new engine is targeted for 2034, with full-scale serial production commencing in 2036. These milestones align with the AMCA program's schedule, which aims for operational induction around 2035-36.

The estimated investment for the engine program is $4.5 to $5 billion, with the Prime Minister's Office overseeing the final selection process.

A Strategic Race

Rolls-Royce's partnership with Reliance places it in direct competition with French defense company Safran, which powers the Indian Air Force's Rafale fighters with its M88 engine. While Safran has also offered technology transfer, analysts have noted that its proposal is based on an enhanced version of the existing M88 — a fourth-generation architecture that may struggle to meet fifth-generation benchmarks like supercruise and low infrared signature.

Rolls-Royce is pitching a clean-sheet design, leveraging over 80 years of engine development expertise. The company has also proposed building a complete aerospace engine ecosystem in India, covering design, production, maintenance, and future upgrades.

India Joins an Elite Club

If the partnership delivers on its promises, India would join the United States, Russia, China, France, and the United Kingdom as one of only a handful of nations capable of designing and manufacturing advanced jet engines. The decision will shape India's aerospace capabilities for decades to come, extending beyond the AMCA to future combat aircraft including potential sixth-generation fighters and the Navy's Twin Engine Deck-Based Fighter.
